claim: The assembly and maintenance of all cilia and flagella require intraflagellar transport (IFT) along the axoneme.
source: The assembly and maintenance of all cilia and flagella require intraflagellar transport (IFT) along the axoneme.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the manuscript's introduction and cited literature.

claim: IFT trains are coupled to flagellar membrane glycoproteins (FMGs) in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: We show that IFT trains are coupled to flagellar membrane glycoproteins (FMGs) in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that IFT pausing and FMG transport depend on Ca2+ concentration (Figure 5).

claim: IFT trains transiently pause through surface adhesion of their FMG cargos.
source: IFT trains transiently pause through surface adhesion of their FMG cargos, and dynein-1b motors pull the cell towards the distal tip of the axoneme.
evidence: This is demonstrated by direct observation of IFT train pausing during gliding motility (Figure 2).

claim: Dynein-1b motors pull the cell towards the distal tip of the axoneme during gliding motility.
source: IFT trains transiently pause through surface adhesion of their FMG cargos, and dynein-1b motors pull the cell towards the distal tip of the axoneme.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that uniflagellate cells glide with the flagellum in the lead and that dynein-1b inhibition reduces gliding (Figure 2C-E).

claim: Each IFT train is transported by at least four motors.
source: Each train is transported by at least four motors, with only one type of motor active at a time.
evidence: This is estimated from optical trap force measurements showing 20-30 pN forces, divided by single motor stall forces of 6-7 pN.

claim: Only one type of motor is active at a time on IFT trains.
source: Each train is transported by at least four motors, with only one type of motor active at a time.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that inactivation of one motor type does not increase forces in the opposite direction (Figure 8).

claim: IFT is a universal mechanism for nearly all eukaryotic cilia and flagella.
source: IFT is a universal mechanism for nearly all eukaryotic cilia and flagella, and defects in this process are linked to a wide range of human diseases, including polycystic kidney disease, retinal degeneration (Rosenbaum and Witman, 2002; Ishikawa and Marshall, 2011), and Bardet-Biedl syndrome (Ou et al., 2005; Lechtreck et al., 2009, 2013; Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Defects in IFT are linked to polycystic kidney disease, retinal degeneration, and Bardet-Biedl syndrome.
source: IFT is a universal mechanism for nearly all eukaryotic cilia and flagella, and defects in this process are linked to a wide range of human diseases, including polycystic kidney disease, retinal degeneration (Rosenbaum and Witman, 2002; Ishikawa and Marshall, 2011), and Bardet-Biedl syndrome (Ou et al., 2005; Lechtreck et al., 2009, 2013; Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: IFT trains make multiple connections with the flagellar membrane.
source: IFT trains make multiple connections with the flagellar membrane (Pigino et al., 2009) and carry several ciliary and flagellar membrane proteins (Qin et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2007; Lechtreck et al., 2009, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: IFT trains carry several ciliary and flagellar membrane proteins.
source: IFT trains make multiple connections with the flagellar membrane (Pigino et al., 2009) and carry several ciliary and flagellar membrane proteins (Qin et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2007; Lechtreck et al., 2009, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies identifying IFT cargo proteins.

claim: Inactivation of kinesin-2 in the fla10ts mutant stops both IFT and gliding motility.
source: Inactivation of kinesin-2 in the temperature-sensitive (ts) mutant fla10ts stops both IFT and gliding motility (Kozminski et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Beads coated with anti-FMG1-B antibody colocalize with IFT trains during processive runs.
source: Figure 1B shows the colocalization of a membrane-attached bead with an individual IFT train as it moves unidirectionally for >500 nm. The movements of the bead and the colocalized IFT trains correlate strongly (>0.99) with each other during the processive run (N = 30, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for more examples)
evidence: This is demonstrated by simultaneous tracking of beads and IFT27-GFP showing strong correlation (>0.99) in their movements.

claim: The correlation between bead and IFT train positions is statistically significant (p=7 × 10−9).
source: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (p=7 × 10−9, Figure 1C) demonstrates that IFT trains colocalize with FMG1-B along the flagellar membrane (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis comparing observed distances to random distribution.

claim: Pausing of retrograde IFT trains is required for the initiation of whole-cell gliding movements.
source: Remarkably, the pausing of IFT trains was required for the initiation of whole-cell movements (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2). We did not observe the start of a gliding event without a paused IFT train.
evidence: This is demonstrated by direct observation of IFT trains during gliding motility initiation.

claim: All paused IFT trains that initiated gliding motility were moving in the retrograde direction.
source: We were able to determine the directionality of 60% of the paused IFT trains, and all of the trains correspondent to the initiation of gliding motility stopped moving during retrograde transport (N = 148).
evidence: This is based on analysis of 148 pausing events associated with gliding initiation.

claim: The average lag time between retrograde IFT pausing and gliding initiation is 0.48 ± 0.05 s.
source: The average lag time was 0.48 ± 0.05 s.
evidence: This is measured from analysis of the timing between IFT pausing and gliding initiation.

claim: Individual IFT pausing events occur every 8.25 ± 0.96 s per cell.
source: In comparison, we observed individual IFT pausing events (including both anterograde and retrograde pauses) every 8.25 ± 0.96 s per cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is measured from analysis of IFT pausing frequency in gliding cells.

claim: The timing of retrograde IFT pausing and gliding motility are not independent (p<0.0001).
source: The Student's t-test excludes the null hypothesis that the timing of retrograde IFT pausing and gliding motility are independent of each other (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis comparing lag time to overall pausing frequency.

claim: Anterograde IFT trains display rare pauses at approximately 0.02 s−1 per cell.
source: Anterograde trains also displayed rare pauses (∼0.02 s−1 per cell, N = 27), but we never observed pausing of an anterograde train before the initiation of gliding motility.
evidence: This is measured from observation of anterograde IFT trains in gliding cells.

claim: Pausing of anterograde trains does not initiate gliding motility.
source: Anterograde trains also displayed rare pauses (∼0.02 s−1 per cell, N = 27), but we never observed pausing of an anterograde train before the initiation of gliding motility.
evidence: This is based on observation of all gliding initiation events.

claim: In 24% of cases, a single paused IFT train is sufficient to pull the entire cell.
source: In 24% of all cases (N = 50), a single paused train appeared sufficient to pull the entire cell (Figure 2A, Video 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of 50 gliding events.

claim: Uniflagellate pf18 cells always glide with the flagellum leading the cell body at 1.49 ± 0.10 µm/s.
source: First, uniflagellate pf18 cells always glided with the flagellum leading the cell body at 1.49 ± 0.10 µm/s (mean ± SEM) (Figure 2C–E, Video 3) (Bloodgood, 2009)
evidence: This is measured from observation of uniflagellate pf18 cell gliding.

claim: Uniflagellate dynein-1b ts cells are unable to display robust gliding at restrictive temperatures.
source: In contrast to pf18 cells, uniflagellate dynein-1b ts cells (dhc1b-3ts) (Engel et al., 2012) were unable to display robust gliding at restrictive temperatures (Figure 2C, Video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by observation of dhc1b-3ts cells at 37°C.

claim: Only 54% of dhc1b-3ts cells display short-range gliding-like motion at restrictive temperatures.
source: We observed only short-range (<500 nm) gliding-like motion in 54% of these cells, compared to robust unidirectional gliding motility observed over 5 µm in pf18 cells.
evidence: This is measured from observation of dhc1b-3ts cells at restrictive temperature.

claim: Short-range gliding motions in dhc1b-3ts cells are bidirectional and significantly slower than pf18 cells.
source: These short-range motions were bidirectional (Figure 2D) and significantly slower (forward: 0.35 ± 0.09 µm/s, backward: 0.47 ± 0.16 µm/s) than the gliding speed of pf18 cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is measured from analysis of dhc1b-3ts cell motility at restrictive temperature.

claim: Inactivation of dynein-1b in biflagellate dhc1b-3ts cells decreased the fraction of gliding cells from 100% to 52%.
source: Second, inactivation of dynein-1b in biflagellate dhc1b-3ts cells decreased the fraction of gliding cells from 100% to 52% and reduced the gliding speed from 0.86 ± 0.08 µm/s to 0.18 ± 0.03 µm/s.
evidence: This is measured by comparing gliding at permissive and restrictive temperatures.

claim: Inactivation of dynein-1b reduced gliding speed from 0.86 ± 0.08 µm/s to 0.18 ± 0.03 µm/s.
source: Second, inactivation of dynein-1b in biflagellate dhc1b-3ts cells decreased the fraction of gliding cells from 100% to 52% and reduced the gliding speed from 0.86 ± 0.08 µm/s to 0.18 ± 0.03 µm/s.
evidence: This is measured by comparing gliding speeds at permissive and restrictive temperatures.

claim: Inactivation of kinesin-2 in fla10ts cells resulted in a twofold increase in gliding speed.
source: In contrast, inactivation of kinesin-2 in fla10ts cells resulted in a twofold increase in gliding speed (Figure 2E), indicating that kinesin plays an inhibitory role during dynein-1b driven gliding motility.
evidence: This is measured by comparing gliding speeds at permissive and restrictive temperatures.

claim: Kinesin-2 plays an inhibitory role during dynein-1b driven gliding motility.
source: In contrast, inactivation of kinesin-2 in fla10ts cells resulted in a twofold increase in gliding speed (Figure 2E), indicating that kinesin plays an inhibitory role during dynein-1b driven gliding motility.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that kinesin-2 inactivation increases gliding speed.

claim: At 150 µM ciliobrevin D, retrograde IFT frequency was reduced by 92%.
source: At 150 µM ciliobrevin D, retrograde IFT frequency was reduced by 92% compared to the 70% decrease observed after 6 hr of heat inactivation of dhc1b-3ts cells (Engel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is measured from analysis of IFT frequency after ciliobrevin D treatment.

claim: Ciliobrevin D treatment reduced retrograde IFT velocity by 60% and anterograde velocity by 36%.
source: The velocities of retrograde and anterograde trains also decreased by 60% and 36%, respectively (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is measured from analysis of IFT velocities after ciliobrevin D treatment.

claim: Inhibition of dynein-1b with ciliobrevin D resulted in 79% reduction in gliding speed and 79% reduction in gliding frequency.
source: Importantly, inhibition of dynein-1b resulted in a significant reduction in the speed (79%) and frequency (79%) of gliding motility (N = 50, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is measured from analysis of gliding motility after ciliobrevin D treatment.

claim: During 60% of gliding reversals, the cell lifts one of its flagella.
source: During 60% of reversals (N = 40), the cell lifted one of its flagella and the paused IFT trains on the surface-adhered flagellum drove the motility (Bloodgood, 2009).
evidence: This is measured from analysis of 40 reversal events.

claim: At normal Ca2+ concentration (0.34 mM), 95% of all surface-adhered cells displayed gliding motility.
source: In regular TAP media (free [Ca2+] = 0.34 mM), 95% of all surface-adhered cells displayed gliding motility and individual pausing events were observed every ∼8 s per flagellum, on average.
evidence: This is measured from observation of cells in normal TAP media.

claim: At <1 µM Ca2+, both the fraction of gliding cells and IFT pausing frequency were reduced by approximately 10-fold.
source: In contrast, both the fraction of gliding cells and IFT pausing frequency were reduced by ∼10-fold at <1 µM Ca2+ (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is measured from analysis of cells in Ca2+-depleted media.

claim: Ca2+ is required for attachment of FMG1-B to IFT trains, not for activation of motor proteins.
source: Thus, we propose that Ca2+ is required for attachment of FMG1-B to IFT trains, not for the activation of a motor protein that provides force for gliding, as previously suggested (Bloodgood, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IFT continues normally without Ca2+ but beads do not move processively.

claim: IFT trains remained colocalized with trapped beads when subjected to external forces.
source: We observed that IFT trains remained colocalized with trapped beads when subjected to external forces (Figure 6B; see Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for additional examples).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simultaneous TIRF imaging and optical trapping.

claim: The average offset between trapped beads and colocalized IFT trains was 280 ± 10 nm.
source: The average offset between the positions of the trapped beads and colocalized IFT trains was 280 ± 10 nm (N = 11).
evidence: This is measured from simultaneous tracking of beads and IFT trains during optical trapping.

claim: Anterograde IFT trains moved against 21.4 ± 0.7 pN peak forces.
source: Histograms of peak forces (Figure 6D) show that anterograde and retrograde IFT trains moved against 21.4 ± 0.7 pN and 25.2 ± 1.3 pN (SEM), respectively.
evidence: This is measured from optical trap force measurements.

claim: Retrograde IFT trains moved against 25.2 ± 1.3 pN peak forces.
source: Histograms of peak forces (Figure 6D) show that anterograde and retrograde IFT trains moved against 21.4 ± 0.7 pN and 25.2 ± 1.3 pN (SEM), respectively.
evidence: This is measured from optical trap force measurements.

claim: 20% of retrograde runs escaped the trap by producing more than 80 pN of force.
source: 20% of retrograde runs escaped the trap by producing more than 80 pN of force, presumably via clustering of FMG1-B (Bloodgood, 2009), while <1% escape events were observed in the anterograde direction.
evidence: This is measured from analysis of optical trap escape events.

claim: Less than 1% of anterograde runs escaped the trap.
source: 20% of retrograde runs escaped the trap by producing more than 80 pN of force, presumably via clustering of FMG1-B (Bloodgood, 2009), while <1% escape events were observed in the anterograde direction.
evidence: This is measured from analysis of optical trap escape events.

claim: The speed of gliding motility (1.49 ± 0.10 µm/s) is significantly slower than that of retrograde IFT (2.96 ± 0.14 µm/s).
source: We next investigated why the speed of gliding motility (1.49 ± 0.10 µm/s, SEM) is significantly slower than that of retrograde IFT (2.96 ± 0.14 µm/s), even though both processes are powered by dynein-1b motors actively transporting IFT trains.
evidence: This is measured from comparison of gliding and IFT speeds.

claim: IFT trains that carry 1-μm beads moved approximately 30% slower than IFT trains not associated with beads.
source: IFT trains that carry 1-μm beads moved ∼30% slower than IFT trains that were not associated with the beads (two-tailed Student's t-test, p = 2.1 × 10−9 (anterograde) and 1.8 × 10−11 (retrograde), Figure 7A).
evidence: This is measured from comparison of IFT speeds with and without beads.

claim: The average drag constant of the bead-IFT complex was 8.0 ± 2.8 pN s/μm.
source: The average drag constant of the bead-IFT complex was found to be 8.0 ± 2.8 pN s/μm (SEM, N = 30).
evidence: This is measured from analysis of bead recoil after stalling in optical trap.

claim: Anterograde and retrograde trains moving at 2–3 µm/s would experience 16–24 pN resistive forces.
source: Anterograde and retrograde trains moving at 2–3 µm/s would experience 16–24 pN resistive forces, comparable to the total motor force exerted on a single IFT train (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is calculated from the measured drag constant and IFT velocity.

claim: Heat-inactivation of kinesin-2 reduced the frequency of anterograde runs by 66% but did not alter the peak forces on retrograde runs.
source: Heat-inactivation of kinesin-2 reduced the frequency of anterograde runs by 66%, but did not alter the peak forces on retrograde runs (Laib et al., 2009) (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is measured from optical trap experiments with fla10-1ts cells at restrictive temperature.

claim: Heat inactivation of dynein-1b significantly reduced the ratio of retrograde to anterograde transport events to 0.15.
source: Similarly, heat inactivation of dynein-1b significantly reduced the ratio of retrograde to anterograde transport events (0.15), but had minimal effect on the peak forces of anterograde runs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is measured from optical trap experiments with dhc1b-3ts cells at restrictive temperature.

claim: Heat inactivation of dynein-1b had minimal effect on the peak forces of anterograde runs.
source: Similarly, heat inactivation of dynein-1b significantly reduced the ratio of retrograde to anterograde transport events (0.15), but had minimal effect on the peak forces of anterograde runs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is measured from optical trap experiments with dhc1b-3ts cells at restrictive temperature.

claim: Only one type of motor remains active on IFT trains at a time.
source: These results exclude a tug-of-war mechanism in IFT, which would lead to an increase of force from motors walking in one direction upon inactivation of the motors walking in the opposite direction. Instead, only one type of a motor remains active on IFT trains at a time, which is consistent with the result that retrograde speed of fla10-1ts does not change after kinesin-2 is inactivated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inactivating one motor type does not increase forces in the opposite direction.

claim: Kinesin-2 on paused anterograde trains slows down gliding motility by exerting forces in the opposite direction to dynein-1b on paused retrograde trains.
source: We propose that kinesin-2 on paused anterograde trains slows down gliding motility by exerting forces in the opposite direction to that of dynein-1b on paused retrograde trains.
evidence: This is proposed to explain why kinesin-2 inactivation increases gliding speed.

claim: IFT trains carry FMG1-B as a cargo in Chlamydomonas.
source: In Chlamydomonas, IFT trains carry FMG1-B as a cargo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization experiments showing beads coated with FMG1-B antibody moving with IFT trains.

claim: The interaction between IFT trains and FMG1-B clusters is transient.
source: The interaction between IFT trains and FMG1-B clusters is transient, as FMG1-B boards moving trains but usually unloads and diffuses away before the trains arrive at the flagellar base or tip.
evidence: This is observed in experiments showing beads transiently associating with and dissociating from IFT trains.

claim: During gliding motility, IFT trains pause due to attachment of the FMG1-B cargo to the surface.
source: During gliding motility, IFT trains pause due to attachment of the FMG1-B cargo to the surface, and the dynein-1b motors engaged to the paused IFT trains generate pulling forces along the microtubule long axis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by observation of IFT pausing during gliding and the requirement of dynein-1b for gliding.

claim: Gliding motility in C. reinhardtii is powered by intracellular transport machinery along microtubules.
source: While the majority of organismal motilities rely on the actin cytoskeleton or axonemal beating, gliding motility in C. reinhardtii is distinct in that it is powered by intracellular transport machinery along microtubules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments showing IFT and dynein-1b drive gliding.

claim: FMG1-B performs an analogous function to integrins in mammalian cell motility.
source: By providing surface adhesion points, FMG1-B performs an analogous function to integrins in mammalian cell motility (Bloodgood, 2009; Lecuit et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an analogy drawn based on the adhesion function of FMG1-B.

claim: Viscous drag of the membrane slows down the motility of IFT trains that carry FMG1-B-conjugated beads.
source: First, we showed that viscous drag of the membrane slows down the motility of IFT trains that carry FMG1-B-conjugated beads, causing gliding motility and FMG1-B transport to proceed slower than IFT.
evidence: This is demonstrated by measurements of drag constants and speed reductions when IFT carries beads.

claim: IFT is unaffected by changes in environmental Ca2+ concentration.
source: Second, previous work showed that IFT is unaffected by changes in environmental Ca2+ concentration (Bloodgood and Salomonsky, 1990; Kozminski et al., 1993), whereas gliding motility is Ca2+-dependent (Bloodgood and Salomonsky, 1990; Kozminski et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Gliding motility is Ca2+-dependent.
source: Second, previous work showed that IFT is unaffected by changes in environmental Ca2+ concentration (Bloodgood and Salomonsky, 1990; Kozminski et al., 1993), whereas gliding motility is Ca2+-dependent (Bloodgood and Salomonsky, 1990; Kozminski et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by experiments in this study.

claim: The presence of free Ca2+ leads to frequent pauses in IFT motility at flagellar adhesion sites.
source: We found that the presence of free Ca2+ leads to frequent pauses in IFT motility at flagellar adhesion sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing increased IFT pausing at normal Ca2+ levels.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, IFT moves unidirectionally without interruptions.
source: In the absence of Ca2+, IFT moves unidirectionally without interruptions, suggesting that attachment of FMG1-B to IFT trains is regulated by a Ca2+-dependent signaling pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing reduced IFT pausing in Ca2+-depleted cells.

claim: Attachment of FMG1-B to IFT trains is regulated by a Ca2+-dependent signaling pathway.
source: In the absence of Ca2+, IFT moves unidirectionally without interruptions, suggesting that attachment of FMG1-B to IFT trains is regulated by a Ca2+-dependent signaling pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ca2+ affects IFT pausing but not IFT movement itself.

claim: Surface adhesion or crosslinking of FMG1-B into large clusters induces dephosphorylation of a transmembrane protein that co-immunoprecipitates with FMG1-B.
source: There is evidence that surface adhesion or crosslinking of FMG1-B into large clusters induces dephosphorylation of a transmembrane protein that co-immunoprecipitates with FMG1-B (Bloodgood and Salomonsky, 1994, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The complex may be regulated by a calcium-calmodulin dependent gliding associated kinase (GAK), which is required for gliding motility.
source: The complex may be regulated by a calcium-calmodulin dependent gliding associated kinase (GAK), which is required for the gliding motility (Bloodgood and Spano, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In a previous trapping assay, beads nonspecifically adsorbed to the flagellar membrane exerted 60 pN average peak forces.
source: In a previous trapping assay, beads nonspecifically adsorbed to the flagellar membrane were found to exert 60 pN average peak forces (Laib et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IFT is required for signal transduction during the mating of ciliated organisms.
source: For example, IFT is required for signal transduction during the mating of ciliated organisms.
evidence: This is stated as an example of IFT's role in signaling.

claim: IFT trains transport sexual agglutinins within the flagellar membrane of gametic cells.
source: Since IFT trains transport sexual agglutinins within the flagellar membrane of gametic cells (Ferris et al., 2005), adhesion between sexual agglutinins of opposite cell types may stall retrograde IFT movement.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Adhesion between sexual agglutinins of opposite cell types may stall retrograde IFT movement.
source: Since IFT trains transport sexual agglutinins within the flagellar membrane of gametic cells (Ferris et al., 2005), adhesion between sexual agglutinins of opposite cell types may stall retrograde IFT movement.
evidence: This is proposed as a mechanism for flagellar alignment during mating.

claim: Microspheres have been observed to move and accumulate at the flagellar tips during mating.
source: Indeed, microspheres have been observed to move and accumulate at the flagellar tips during mating (Hoffman and Goodenough, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cilia in the retina, liver, and kidney cells make direct physical contacts that may serve as 'bridges' for signaling networks between many cells.
source: Cilia in the retina, liver, and kidney cells were recently observed to make direct physical contacts, which may serve as 'bridges' for signaling networks between many cells (Ott et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: These contacts are tight adhesions between the ciliary membranes, mediated by N-linked glycoproteins.
source: These contacts are tight adhesions between the ciliary membranes, mediated by N-linked glycoproteins.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of ciliary contacts.

claim: IFT may exert force on cell-cell adhesion sites and determine the positioning of these adhesion sites by moving them along the length of the cilium.
source: It is possible that IFT exerts force on cell-cell adhesion sites and determines the positioning of these adhesion sites by moving them along the length of the cilium.
evidence: This is proposed as a potential mechanism based on the findings of this study.

claim: Ca2+ signaling at flagellar adhesion sites may play a major role in regulating attachment to IFT trains and controlling the direction of force generation.
source: Ca2+ signaling at flagellar adhesion sites may play a major role in regulating attachment to IFT trains and controlling the direction of force generation.
evidence: This is proposed based on the Ca2+-dependent nature of IFT pausing and gliding.
